cognate: Gk λείπω = Lat (re)linquo < *leykʷ- 'leave', in a death expression whose object is 'the light' (of life/of the eyes); eye-words *h₃ekʷ- in both slab passages
drift_or_renewal: renewal of the noun: Gk φάος (*bʰeh₂-) vs Lat lumen (*lewk-); in the slab's Homeric anchor the subject is renewed (ψυχή leaves the man, cf. h.Ven. 272 ψυχὴ λείπει φάος) while the Latin keeps man-leaves-light
shared_syntax: verb 'leave' + accusative 'light' with the dying person as subject (Gk λείπειν φάος ἠελίοιο; Lat lumina (re)linquere), a euphemism for dying
context: Il. 5.696: Sarpedon faints, 'the soul left him and mist poured over his eyes'; Lucr. 3.1025 quotes Ennius (Ann.) on the death of Ancus, 'even good Ancus left the light with his eyes'. Both are epic death statements built on leave + eyes/light; in Greek the full formula λείπειν φάος ἠελίοιο is formulaic in Homer, Hesiod, h.Ven. and Theognis, and Lucretius uses lumina linquere three more times. The Latin verb is the poetic linquo, not a neutral 'go away', which makes a chance convergence of verb choice somewhat less likely; but 'light = life' is a widespread metaphor and 'leave' is the obvious verb, so the match could be independent.
phrase: *leykʷ- + 'light' = 'to die' (Gk λείπειν φάος ἠελίοιο ~ Enn./Lucr. lumina (re)linquere)

search_lead.cognate: ON ljá / OS farlīhan 'lend, grant' < *leykʷ- + ON ljós / OS lioht < *lewk-; cf. Lat lumina relinquere
search_lead.argument: In two Germanic blind-healing miracles God/Christ 'grants (lends) light' to the blind: ON 'léði guð honum ljós', OS Heliand 'farlīhi theses liohtes'. Same root pair as Latin lumina (re)linquere 'die', with Germanic's known drift of *leykʷ- to 'lend'. The sense runs the other way (granting sight vs leaving life), both texts are Christian, and l-alliteration alone could account for the Germanic pairing; I do not claim it as inherited.

near_miss.lead: ON leðe guð hanum lios ~ Lat lumina ... oculis reliquit (*leykʷ- + *lewk-)
near_miss.why_not: The sense is reversed (God grants sight to a blind man, vs. a man leaves the light and dies), the text is a Christian miracle, and Germanic l-alliteration explains the pair; filed as a search lead (Heliand 3576) rather than a claim.

near_miss.lead: oculos suffusa luce ~ κατὰ δ' ὀφθαλμῶν κέχυτ' ἀχλύς (*ǵʰew- 'pour' + eyes)
near_miss.why_not: The Latin is a medical description of bloodshot eyes in the plague, not a death or fainting formula; 'pour over the eyes' is ordinary in both languages.

near_miss.lead: gods and men: ræddezk hvarke guð ne menn; mote guðs lagum oc manna ~ AV pitṛbhir ... manuṣyaiḥ
near_miss.why_not: The ON is a biblical/legal calque (Luke 18:2 'Deum non timebat nec hominem reverebatur'; 'lex Dei et hominum'). The AV pairs fathers and men, not gods, and the Greek partners hold nothing comparable.
A kinship pair that comes up in any family context. The contexts (two brothers and their sister; Yama–Yamī dialogue; a legal letter) share no wording beyond the two nouns.
Biblical simile (Matt 28:3, Dan 7:9). The Latin nix cana is not a simile, and the colour words are not cognate.

near_miss.lead: tears (*dáḱru) + mother: með tarom ... mæy mariu drotens moðor ~ δάκρυ χέων ... πότνια μήτηρ
near_miss.why_not: ON 'með tárum' is Latin 'cum lacrimis' prayer phraseology. The mother is the addressee of the prayer, not the one weeping, and there is no verb 'pour'.

near_miss.lead: sun + darkness: solen fal gæisla sinn oc gerðe myrct ~ Сунце зађе, мрак на земљу паде
near_miss.why_not: The ON is an eclipse miracle explicitly modelled on the crucifixion darkness, and the Vuk lines are an ordinary sunset formula. The words for darkness are not securely cognate (myrkr / mrak only possibly), and the contexts differ.

near_miss.lead: sun + *sḱeh₁i- 'shine' negated: æigi nar sol at skina ~ јошт није обасјало сунце
near_miss.why_not: Cognate sun + shine, but 'the sun shines' is everyday language. The contexts differ: an omen of the sun failing at Stiklestad, vs dawn not yet broken.

near_miss.lead: good/bad at heart: Gott er þessom karle um hiartat ~ durhārd hṛdayena
near_miss.why_not: The ON is Þormóðr's literal remark about the fat on the heart around the arrow, not a moral epithet. The Vedic compound has no Norse counterpart.

near_miss.lead: tongue (*dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s) healed/vigorous: Tungan var nu hæil ~ uox et lingua uigeret
near_miss.why_not: Only 'tongue' is shared: the ON is a healing miracle and the Latin is on the origin of language. The other tongue partners (PlAsina 512, AV 5.30, MBh) are unrelated.

near_miss.lead: hunted by hounds: ocom ditin ar chonaib altaib ~ fara æftir hanum ... með hunda
near_miss.why_not: Shared 'dog' only. Tuan mac Cairill fleeing wolves, vs a runaway tracked by dogs; generic.

near_miss.lead: spear through shield and three ribs to the heart (scíath ... trí asna ... cride)
near_miss.why_not: No partner continues the wounding run; the two Irish partners are versions of the same Táin passage, not independent witnesses. Read closely; nothing found in BS-12765, BS-50285, BS-9a658, BS-a10f2, BS-7fbc8, BS-04895, BS-dae75 or BS-f5acc either (shared roots only).
